cards.label: Question 1 · 3 marks · Section A
cards.title: Question 1
cards.q: Distinguish between the subdisciplines of "materials science" and "materials engineering". State the four components of the central paradigm of materials science and engineering.

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you distinguish materials science from materials engineering?

options.t: Both distinguished: science finds structure-property links, engineering designs structure
Only one of the two fields defined, or the distinction is vague
Both defined wrongly, or the distinction not attempted

cards.why: Full marks need science as discovering structure-property relationships and engineering as designing structure for set properties.

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you name all four components of the paradigm?

options.t: All four named: processing, structure, properties and performance
Three of the four components named
Fewer than three components named, or none

cards.why: Full marks need all four components: processing, structure, properties and performance.

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you show how the components link, in order?

options.t: Chain given in order, with a short explanation of each link
Components listed, but no order or link between them
No paradigm given, or the chain is out of order

cards.why: Processing changes structure, structure controls properties, and properties determine performance.

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 3
cards.title: Materials science
cards.body: Materials science discovers the relationships between the structure of a material and its properties.

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 3
cards.title: Materials engineering
cards.body: Materials engineering designs or engineers the structure of a material to obtain a predetermined set of properties.

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 3
cards.title: Central paradigm
cards.body: The paradigm has four linked components: processing, structure, properties and performance. Processing changes structure, structure determines properties, and properties determine performance.

cards.body: The four linked components of materials science and engineering.

cards.title: Remember
points: Materials science: discover structure-property relationships
Materials engineering: design structure to obtain set properties
Paradigm: processing, structure, properties, performance
Processing changes structure; structure controls properties
Properties determine performance in service

cards.q: Materials science discovers relationships between structure and ____.
cards.why: Materials science explains how a material's structure determines its properties.
cards.label: Remember · word check 1 of 3

cards.q: Changing the processing of a material first changes its ____.
cards.why: Processing changes structure; the changed structure controls properties.
cards.label: Remember · word check 2 of 3

cards.q: The stage of the materials paradigm that describes behaviour in service is ____.
cards.why: Performance describes how a material functions in its service environment.
cards.label: Remember · word check 3 of 3
Question 2 · 3 marks · Section A
cards.title: Question 2
cards.q: What are the three primary criteria that engineers and scientists must consider when selecting a material for a specific engineering application?

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you name the in-service conditions criterion?

options.t: Named in-service conditions with the property needs, e.g. strength or temperature
Criterion named, but no property requirements given
Criterion not named

cards.why: Full marks need in-service conditions named with the property requirements the material must meet in use.

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you name deterioration of properties during service?

options.t: Named deterioration in service with examples such as corrosion, wear or creep
Deterioration mentioned, without examples
Deterioration not mentioned

cards.why: Full marks need deterioration in service named, with examples such as corrosion, wear or creep.

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you name economics as the third criterion?

options.t: Named economics, referring to the cost of the finished component
Cost mentioned, but not linked to the component
Economics not mentioned

cards.why: Full marks need economics named, meaning the cost of the finished component.

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 3
cards.title: Three criteria
cards.body: The three primary criteria are in-service conditions, deterioration of material properties during service, and economics.

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 3
cards.title: In-service conditions
cards.body: These are the property requirements the material must meet in use, such as strength and the operating temperature.

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 3
cards.title: Deterioration and economics
cards.body: The material must resist deterioration such as corrosion, wear and creep. The cost of the finished component must also be acceptable.

cards.label: Key points
cards.title: Remember
points: Three criteria: in-service conditions, deterioration, economics
In-service conditions: required properties such as strength and temperature
Deterioration: corrosion, wear and creep during service
Economics: cost of the finished component
Material choice balances all three, not just one

cards.q: Corrosion and wear are examples of material ____ during service.
cards.why: Deterioration includes corrosion, wear and creep during use.
cards.label: Remember · word check 1 of 3

cards.q: The selection criterion concerned with the finished component's cost is ____.
cards.why: Economics includes the cost of producing the finished component.
cards.label: Remember · word check 2 of 3

cards.q: Required strength is a property specified by the material's service ____.
cards.why: In-service conditions determine the properties the component needs.
cards.label: Remember · word check 3 of 3
Question 3 · 3 marks · Section A
cards.title: Question 3
cards.q: What are composites? How do metals differ from ceramics in terms of atomic bonding and mechanical properties?

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you define a composite?

options.t: Two or more distinct materials combined, with an example such as fibreglass or concrete
Defined as two or more materials, with no example
Not defined, or the definition is wrong

cards.why: Full marks need a composite as two or more distinct materials combined for the best properties, with an example.

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you explain metallic bonding and the properties of metals?

options.t: Metallic bonding with delocalised electrons, linked to strength and ductility
Metallic bonding named, but no delocalised electrons
Bonding not described, or wrongly described

cards.why: Metals have metallic bonding from delocalised electrons, giving strength, ductility, conductivity and toughness.

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you contrast ceramics: bonding and properties?

options.t: Ionic or covalent bonding, with hard, brittle, insulating properties
Bonding or properties given, but not both
Neither bonding nor properties given

cards.why: Ceramics have ionic or covalent bonding, giving hard, brittle, insulating, high melting behaviour.

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 3
cards.title: Composites
cards.body: A composite is an engineered material made from two or more distinct materials, combined to give the best properties of each. Examples are fibreglass, carbon fibre and concrete.

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 3
cards.title: Metals
cards.body: Metals have metallic bonding, with delocalised electrons. This makes them strong, ductile, electrically conducting and tough.

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 3
cards.title: Ceramics
cards.body: Ceramics have ionic or covalent bonding. This makes them hard, brittle, insulating and high melting, unlike metals.

cards.label: Key points
cards.title: Remember
points: Composite: two or more distinct materials combined for best properties
Metals: metallic bonding with delocalised electrons
Metals are strong, ductile, conducting and tough
Ceramics: ionic or covalent bonding
Ceramics are hard, brittle, insulating and high melting

cards.q: A material combining distinct constituents to obtain useful properties is a ____.
cards.why: A composite combines two or more distinct materials for useful combined properties.
cards.label: Remember · word check 1 of 3

cards.q: The ability of a metal to undergo substantial plastic deformation is called ____.
cards.why: Metals are commonly ductile: they can deform plastically before fracture.
cards.label: Remember · word check 2 of 3

cards.q: Compared with ductile metals, ceramics are typically ____.
cards.why: Ceramics are generally hard and brittle because of their ionic or covalent bonding.
cards.label: Remember · word check 3 of 3
Question 4 · 3 marks · Section A
cards.title: Question 4
cards.q: Define smart materials. What are the two essential components of a smart material system, and what functions do they perform?

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you define a smart material?

options.t: Responds to the environment in a controlled way, with examples
Responds to the environment, but control not stated
Definition missing or wrong

cards.why: Full marks need a smart material defined as responding to the environment in a controlled way, with an example.

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you name the sensor and its function?

options.t: Sensor named, and its role given: it detects the signal
Sensor named, but its role not stated
Sensor not named

cards.why: The sensor detects the signal in a smart material system.

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you name the actuator and its function?

options.t: Actuator named, and its role given: it performs the response or adaptation
Actuator named, but its role not stated
Actuator not named

cards.why: The actuator performs the response or adaptation in a smart material system.

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 2
cards.title: Smart materials
cards.body: Smart materials respond to changes in the environment in a controlled way. Examples include shape-memory alloys, piezoelectric ceramics and magnetostrictive materials.

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 2
cards.title: Two essential components
cards.body: A smart material system has a sensor, which detects the input signal, and an actuator, which performs the response or adaptation.

cards.title: Smart system
cards.body: Sensor and actuator are the two essential components.

cards.label: Key points
cards.title: Remember
points: Smart material: responds to the environment in a controlled way
Sensor: detects the signal
Actuator: performs the response or adaptation
Examples: shape-memory alloys, piezoelectric ceramics, magnetostrictive

cards.q: The component of a smart system that detects a signal is the ____.
cards.why: A sensor detects a change or signal from the environment.
cards.label: Remember · word check 1 of 3

cards.q: The component that carries out a smart material's response is the ____.
cards.why: An actuator performs the response or adaptation.
cards.label: Remember · word check 2 of 3

cards.q: A smart material responds to environmental changes in a ____ way.
cards.why: A controlled response to environmental change is the defining feature of a smart material.
cards.label: Remember · word check 3 of 3
Question 5 · 3 marks · Section A
cards.title: Question 5
cards.q: Define bonding energy \(E_0\) between two atoms in a solid. How do the magnitude of \(E_0\) and the shape of the potential energy curve influence the melting temperature and thermal expansion of a material?

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you define the bonding energy \(E_0\)?

options.t: Energy to separate atoms from \(r_0\) to infinity, the depth of the U(r) minimum
Called bonding energy, but the separation or minimum not explained
Not defined, or the definition is wrong

cards.why: Full marks need \(E_0\) as the energy to separate the atoms from \(r_0\) to infinity, the depth of the minimum.

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you link a larger \(E_0\) to the melting temperature?

options.t: Larger \(E_0\) gives higher melting temperature, because more energy breaks the bonds
Larger \(E_0\) gives higher melting temperature, with no reason
Link not made, or reversed

cards.why: Full marks need a larger \(E_0\) linked to a higher melting temperature, with the reason.

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you link the shape of the well to thermal expansion?

options.t: Deeper, narrower, steeper well linked to lower thermal expansion
Well shape mentioned, but the link to expansion is unclear
No link to expansion, or a wrong link

cards.why: A deeper, narrower, steeper and more symmetric well gives lower thermal expansion.

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 3
cards.title: Bonding energy
cards.body: The bonding energy \(E_0\) is the energy needed to separate two atoms from their equilibrium separation \(r_0\) to infinity. It is the depth of the minimum of the potential energy curve \(U(r)\).

cards.title: Potential energy curve
cards.body: The depth of the minimum is the bond energy \(E_0\); the minimum sits at \(r_0\).
cards.label: Figure
Model answer 2 of 3
cards.title: Melting temperature
cards.body: A larger \(E_0\) means stronger bonds, so more thermal energy is needed to break them, and the melting temperature is higher.

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 3
cards.title: Thermal expansion
cards.body: A deeper, narrower and steeper well, which is more symmetric, gives lower thermal expansion. See the figure of the potential energy curve.

cards.title: Deep or shallow well
cards.body: A deep, narrow well: high melting temperature and low thermal expansion.
cards.label: Figure
Key points
cards.title: Remember
points: E0: energy to separate two atoms from r0 to infinity
E0 is the depth of the minimum of the U(r) curve
Larger E0 gives higher melting temperature
Deeper, narrower, steeper well gives lower thermal expansion

cards.q: The bond energy corresponds to the ____ of the potential-energy minimum.
cards.why: Bond energy is the energy needed to separate equilibrium atoms to infinity, equal to the well depth.
cards.label: Remember · word check 1 of 3

cards.q: Atoms must be separated to ____ to define their full bonding energy.
cards.why: Bonding energy is measured from equilibrium separation to infinite separation.
cards.label: Remember · word check 2 of 3

cards.q: A larger bonding energy generally corresponds to a ____ melting temperature.
cards.why: Stronger bonds require more energy to disrupt, giving a higher melting temperature.
cards.label: Remember · word check 3 of 3
Question 6 · 3 marks · Section A
cards.title: Question 6
cards.q: Explain metallic bonding in crystals using the electron cloud model. Why are metals good conductors of electricity and heat based on their bonding nature?

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you describe the electron cloud model?

options.t: Valence electrons delocalised into a cloud shared by the positive ion cores
Electron cloud or sea mentioned, but not shared by the ion cores
Bonding described as ionic or covalent, or not described

cards.why: Full marks need valence electrons delocalised into a cloud shared by the positive ion cores.

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you state that the metallic bond is non-directional?

options.t: Bond stated as non-directional, with the electron cloud as the reason
Non-directional stated, with no reason
Non-directional not stated

cards.why: A metallic bond is non-directional because the electron cloud is shared equally in all directions.

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you explain conduction by the free electrons?

options.t: Free electrons carry charge and heat, so metals conduct well
Metals conduct, but the free electrons are not mentioned
Conduction not explained, or explained wrongly

cards.why: Full marks need the free electrons carrying charge and heat, so metals are good conductors.

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 3
cards.title: Metallic bonding
cards.body: In metals the valence electrons are delocalised into an electron cloud, shared by the positive ion cores. The bond is non-directional. See the figure of the electron cloud.

cards.title: Electron cloud
cards.body: Free electrons surround the positive ion cores; the bond is non-directional.

cards.title: Non-directional bond
cards.body: Because the electron cloud is not tied to any particular direction, the bond does not depend on direction.

cards.q: In a metallic bond, valence electrons are ____.
cards.why: Valence electrons form a shared, delocalised electron cloud around the positive ion cores.

cards.why: The shared electron cloud is not restricted to particular bond directions.

Question 7 · 3 marks · Section A
cards.title: Question 7
cards.q: What are van der Waals forces? Explain what a permanent dipole bond is and how it affects intermolecular interactions.

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you define van der Waals forces?

options.t: Weak secondary bonds from electric dipoles, with at least one type named
Weak bonds named, but dipole origin not given
Not defined, or confused with primary bonds

cards.why: Full marks need van der Waals forces defined as weak secondary bonds from electric dipoles, with the types named.

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you explain the permanent dipole bond?

options.t: Molecules with permanent dipoles attract each other, with HCl as an example
Permanent dipole named, but not explained
Permanent dipole bond not explained

cards.why: A permanent dipole bond forms between molecules with permanent dipoles, such as HCl.

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you state the effect on intermolecular interactions?

options.t: Sets melting and boiling points; hydrogen bonding is strongest, with H bonded to F, O or N
Effect on melting or boiling point stated, but no hydrogen bonding
No effect given

cards.why: Full marks need the effect on melting and boiling points, and hydrogen bonding as the strongest permanent dipole bond.

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 3
cards.title: van der Waals forces
cards.body: These are weak secondary bonds arising from electric dipoles. They include fluctuating induced dipoles, polar molecule-induced dipoles and permanent dipoles.

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 3
cards.title: Permanent dipole bond
cards.body: A permanent dipole bond forms between molecules that have permanent dipoles, as in HCl. Hydrogen bonding is the strongest permanent dipole bond, where hydrogen is bonded to F, O or N.

cards.title: Permanent dipole bond
cards.body: Two polar molecules attract: the positive end of one pulls the negative end of the other.

cards.title: Effect
cards.body: These forces set the melting and boiling points, and the intermolecular attraction, of molecular solids.

cards.label: Key points
cards.title: Remember
points: van der Waals forces: weak secondary bonds from electric dipoles
Permanent dipole bond: between molecules with permanent dipoles, e.g. HCl
Hydrogen bonding is the strongest permanent dipole bond (H to F, O, N)
These forces set melting and boiling points of molecular solids

cards.q: Van der Waals interactions are classed as ____ bonds.
cards.why: Van der Waals forces are weak secondary interactions associated with electric dipoles.
cards.label: Remember · word check 1 of 3

cards.q: A bond between molecules that already possess dipoles involves ____ dipoles.
cards.why: Molecules such as HCl possess permanent electric dipoles.
cards.label: Remember · word check 2 of 3

cards.q: The relatively strong secondary interaction involving hydrogen bonded to oxygen is ____ bonding.
cards.why: Hydrogen bonding occurs when hydrogen attached to F, O or N interacts with a suitable neighbouring atom.
cards.label: Remember · word check 3 of 3
Question 8 · 3 marks · Section A
cards.title: Question 8
cards.q: Why does solid ice have a lower density than liquid water at room temperature? State two familiar natural or practical consequences of this anomalous volume expansion upon freezing.

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you describe the open structure of ice?

options.t: Four hydrogen bonds per molecule, in an open tetrahedral network with empty space
Hydrogen bonding mentioned, but no open network or empty space
No hydrogen bonding or structure given

cards.why: Full marks need each molecule hydrogen bonded to four neighbours in an open network with empty space.

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you explain why liquid water is denser?

options.t: Network partly collapses on melting, so the liquid is denser by about 9 percent
Liquid stated as denser, but no reason from the structure
Not stated

cards.why: Full marks need the network partly collapsing on melting, making liquid water about 9 percent denser.

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you give two consequences of the expansion?

options.t: Two consequences with reasons, from ice floating, burst pipes or frost weathering
One consequence given, with an explanation
No consequence given, or a wrong one

cards.why: Two consequences, such as ice floating so aquatic life survives, or burst pipes, or frost weathering of rocks.

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 3
cards.title: Structure of ice
cards.body: In ice each water molecule hydrogen bonds to four neighbours, forming an open hexagonal tetrahedral network with empty space. See the small figure of ice and liquid water.

cards.title: Ice and liquid

cards.title: Question 10
cards.q: Define anisotropy in crystalline materials. How is the directionality of properties related to atomic spacing and crystal symmetry?

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you define anisotropy?

options.t: Properties depend on the crystallographic direction, with an example
Direction dependence stated, but no example
Not defined, or wrongly defined

cards.why: Full marks need anisotropy defined as properties depending on the crystallographic direction, with an example.

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you explain the cause of anisotropy?

options.t: Atomic spacing and packing density differ along different directions
Atomic arrangement mentioned, but no spacing or density
No cause given

Symmetry mentioned, but its effect on anisotropy not stated
Symmetry not mentioned

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 3
cards.title: Anisotropy
cards.body: Anisotropy means that properties depend on the crystallographic direction in which they are measured. Elastic modulus and electrical conductivity are examples.

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 3
cards.title: Cause
cards.body: It arises because atomic spacing and packing density differ along different directions in the crystal.

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 3
cards.title: Symmetry
cards.body: High crystal symmetry, as in cubic crystals, reduces anisotropy. Polycrystals with randomly oriented grains are isotropic on average.

cards.label: Key points
cards.title: Remember
points: Anisotropy: properties depend on crystallographic direction
Cause: atomic spacing and packing density vary with direction
High symmetry (cubic) reduces anisotropy
Random polycrystals are isotropic on average

cards.why: Anisotropy means that a measured property changes with crystallographic direction.

cards.why: The directional responses of random grains average out on a macroscopic scale.
cards.label: Remember · word check 2 of 3

cards.why: Atomic spacing and atomic packing vary between crystallographic directions.

cards.title: Question 11
cards.q: Discuss the modern materials' needs in solar energy conversion, transportation, hydrogen fuel cells, and environmental quality. Why is it important to consider the "cradle-to-grave" life cycle of materials?

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 4 · up to 2 marks
cards.q: Did you discuss the needs in solar energy and transportation?

options.t: Both covered: efficient, cheap photovoltaics and light, strong, efficient transport materials
Only one of solar or transport covered, with a reason
Neither covered, or no material need given

cards.why: Full marks need the solar need (efficient, cheap photovoltaics) and the transport need (light, strong, efficient materials).

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 4 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you discuss fuel cells and environmental quality?

options.t: Fuel cells (membranes, catalysts, storage) and environment (recycling, emissions) both given
Only one of these two areas covered
Neither area covered

cards.why: Fuel cells need membranes, catalysts and storage materials; environmental quality needs recycling and reduced emissions.

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 4 · up to 2 marks
cards.q: Did you explain the cradle-to-grave life cycle?

options.t: Extraction, processing, use and disposal or recycling all listed, linked to impact
Life cycle stated with two or three stages named
Only a general mention of the environment, no life cycle

cards.why: A full answer names all four stages (extraction, processing, use, disposal or recycling) and links them to impact.

cards.label: Mark yourself 4 of 4 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you give the reason the life cycle matters?

options.t: Stated that considering every stage reduces total environmental impact
Reason given, but vague and not linked to impact
No reason given

cards.why: The reason is that looking at one stage can shift the environmental cost to another stage.

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 5
cards.title: Solar energy and transport
cards.body: Solar energy conversion needs efficient, cheap photovoltaic materials. Transportation needs materials that are light, strong and efficient, so that vehicles use less energy.

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 5
cards.title: Fuel cells and environment
cards.body: Hydrogen fuel cells need membranes, catalysts and hydrogen storage materials. Environmental quality needs recycling and reduced emissions, so materials must be designed for reuse.

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 5
cards.title: Cradle-to-grave view
cards.body: The cradle-to-grave view follows a material through extraction, processing, use and disposal or recycling. Each stage has an environmental cost, so all stages must be considered.

cards.label: Model answer 4 of 5
cards.title: Why the whole life cycle matters
cards.body: Looking at one stage alone can move the problem elsewhere, for example a light material that is hard to recycle. Considering the whole life cycle reduces the total environmental impact.

cards.label: Model answer 5 of 5
cards.title: Conclusion
cards.body: Good materials design therefore balances performance with energy use, recyclability and emissions across the full life cycle, not only at the point of use.

cards.title: Remember
points: Solar: efficient, cheap photovoltaics. Transport: light, strong, efficient materials.

Environment needs recycling and reduced emissions.
Cradle-to-grave: extraction, processing, use, disposal or recycling.
Whole life cycle must be considered so one stage does not shift impact elsewhere.

cards.title: Question 12
cards.q: Explain how the optical transmittance properties (transparency, translucency, and opacity) of aluminum oxide (\(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\)) disk specimens depend on their internal structure and processing. What is a semiconducting material, and what is its significance?

Two of the three specimens correctly linked to structure

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 4 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you explain why light is scattered in the polycrystal?

options.t: Scattering at grain boundaries and at pores explained
Only grain boundaries or only pores mentioned
No reason for scattering given

cards.why: Light is scattered by grain boundaries in the fine-grained polycrystal and by pores in the porous disk.

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 4 · up to 2 marks
cards.q: Did you define a semiconducting material?

options.t: Conductivity between conductors and insulators, set by doping and temperature, with examples
Intermediate conductivity stated, no doping or temperature control
Definition missing or wrong, for example a good conductor

options.t: Basis of modern electronics: diodes, transistors, integrated circuits, solar cells
Said to be useful in electronics, no examples

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 4
cards.title: Single crystal
cards.body: Single-crystal sapphire is transparent. The lattice is perfectly ordered, so there are no grain boundaries or pores to scatter light, and light passes straight through.

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 4
cards.title: Polycrystalline and porous
cards.body: Fully dense polycrystalline \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\) is translucent, because its fine grains scatter light at the grain boundaries. With about 5 percent porosity the pores scatter light strongly, so the disk is opaque.

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 4
cards.title: Semiconducting material
cards.body: A semiconducting material has electrical conductivity between that of conductors and insulators. Its conductivity can be controlled by doping and by temperature. Examples are silicon, germanium and gallium arsenide.

cards.label: Model answer 4 of 4
cards.title: Significance
cards.body: Semiconductors are the basis of all modern electronics, including diodes, transistors and integrated circuits. They are also used in solar cells.

Question 13 · 6 marks · Section B
cards.title: Question 13
cards.q: Explain the concept of bonding forces and energies in solids. The potential energy between two atoms in a solid is given by \(U(r) = -\frac{A}{r} + \frac{B}{r^n}\), where \(A\) and \(B\) are constants, and \(r\) is the interatomic distance. Explain what happens to the energy when \(r\) increases or decreases, and derive the expression for the equilibrium bond length \(r_0\).

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 4 · up to 2 marks
cards.q: Did you explain the two bonding terms and the energy minimum?

options.t: Attractive term dominates at large r, repulsive at small r, minimum at r0, on a U(r) curve
Both terms named, but no dominance or minimum described
Only one term named, or no explanation

cards.why: Attraction dominates at large separation, repulsion at small separation, and the energy minimum is at r0.

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 4 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you describe how the energy changes as r increases or decreases?

options.t: Energy rises towards zero as r increases, and rises steeply as r decreases
Direction of change given, but no reason from the terms
No description of the change

cards.why: Explain that the attractive term controls the rise to zero at large r, and the repulsive term the steep rise at small r.

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 4 · up to 2 marks
cards.q: Did you derive the equilibrium bond length r0?

options.t: dU/dr set to zero, giving r0 = (nB/A) to the power 1/(n-1)
dU/dr set to zero, but an algebra error in r0
Derivative not taken, or no equilibrium condition used

cards.why: Set dU/dr = A/r squared - nB/r to the power n+1 equal to zero, then solve for r0.

cards.label: Mark yourself 4 of 4 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you state the energy and force at r0?

options.t: U(r0) is negative and equals minus E0, and the force is zero at r0
Only one of the two stated
Neither stated

cards.why: At r0 the energy is minimum and negative, equal to minus the bond energy E0, and the force is zero.

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 3
cards.title: Bonding forces
cards.body: Atoms in a solid are held by an attractive term that dominates at large separations and a repulsive term that dominates at short separations. The total potential energy is written as shown.

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 3
cards.title: Energy as r changes
cards.body: As r increases beyond r0, the attractive term dominates and the energy rises towards zero. As r decreases, the repulsive term dominates and the energy rises steeply. The minimum lies at r0, see the figure.

cards.body: Attraction (dashed), repulsion (dashed) and the total curve, with the minimum at \(r_0\).

Model answer 3 of 3
cards.title: Equilibrium bond length
cards.body: The minimum is where dU/dr is zero, which gives the equilibrium bond length \(r_0\). The energy at \(r_0\) is \(U(r_0) = -E_0\), where \(E_0\) is the bond energy, and the force is zero there. See the derivation.

ask.why: Repulsion rises steeply as the atoms are pushed together.

points: U(r) = -A/r + B/r^n: attractive term at large r, repulsive term at small r.

cards.why: The potential has zero slope at equilibrium, so its associated net force vanishes.

cards.title: Definition
cards.body: Nanocrystalline solids, or nanomaterials, are solids whose grain or particle size lies between about 1 and 100 nm. Their structure is controlled at the nanometre scale.

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 5
cards.title: Top-down approach
cards.body: The top-down approach starts from a bulk material and breaks it down into nanoscale pieces. Examples are milling, lithography and etching.

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 5
cards.title: Bottom-up approach
cards.body: The bottom-up approach builds the material up from atoms or molecules. Examples are chemical vapour deposition, sol-gel processing and self-assembly.

cards.title: Two routes
cards.body: Top-down breaks bulk material down; bottom-up builds nanoparticles from atoms.

cards.label: Model answer 4 of 5
cards.title: Surface-to-volume ratio
cards.body: As particle size falls, the fraction of atoms at the surface rises sharply. This high surface-to-volume ratio makes the material more reactive.

cards.label: Model answer 5 of 5
cards.title: Quantum and grain-boundary effects
cards.body: When size is comparable to the electron wavelength, quantum confinement changes electronic and optical behaviour. Many atoms also sit at grain boundaries, changing colour, melting point and strength.

cards.label: Key points
cards.title: Remember
points: Nanocrystalline: grain or particle size about 1 to 100 nm.
Top-down: break bulk down by milling, lithography or etching.
Bottom-up: assemble atoms by CVD, sol-gel or self-assembly.
High surface-to-volume ratio and quantum confinement change properties.
Many atoms at grain boundaries alter melting point, colour and strength.

cards.q: Breaking a bulk material down into nanoscale pieces is a ____ approach.
cards.why: Milling, lithography and etching are examples of top-down fabrication.
cards.label: Remember · word check 1 of 3

cards.q: Assembling a nanomaterial from atoms or molecules is a ____ approach.
cards.why: Bottom-up fabrication builds larger structures from smaller building blocks.
cards.label: Remember · word check 2 of 3

cards.q: Changes caused by restricting electrons to nanoscale dimensions are associated with quantum ____.
cards.why: Quantum confinement can alter the electronic and optical properties of nanomaterials.
cards.label: Remember · word check 3 of 3
Question 19 · 10 marks · Section C
cards.title: Question 19
cards.q: Classify solid materials into metals, ceramics, polymers, and composites based on their chemical makeup and atomic structure. Compare their density, mechanical (stiffness, strength, fracture toughness), electrical, and optical properties with suitable examples, and discuss the four classes of advanced materials used in high-technology applications.

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 6 · up to 2 marks
cards.q: Did you classify solids by chemical makeup and atomic structure?

options.t: Four classes (metals, ceramics, polymers, composites) linked to bonding and structure
Four classes named, but no link to bonding or structure
Classes incomplete or not given

cards.why: Classify into metals, ceramics, polymers and composites, linking each to its bonding and atomic structure.

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 6 · up to 2 marks
cards.q: Did you give an example for each class?

options.t: Each class with an example: iron, Al2O3, polyethylene, glass-fibre composite
Examples given for only two or three classes
No examples given

cards.why: Examples: iron or aluminium (metals), Al2O3 or SiO2 (ceramics), polyethylene or nylon (polymers), glass fibre in polymer (composite).

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 6 · up to 2 marks
cards.q: Did you compare density and mechanical properties?

options.t: Density and stiffness, strength, toughness compared, with an example for each class
Mechanical properties compared, but no examples
Density or mechanical properties missing

cards.why: Polymers are least dense; metals are stiff, strong and tough; ceramics are stiff but brittle with low toughness.

cards.label: Mark yourself 4 of 6 · up to 2 marks
cards.q: Did you compare electrical and optical properties?

options.t: Metals conduct and are opaque; ceramics and polymers insulate; some ceramics are transparent
Electrical properties given for some classes only
Electrical or optical properties missing

cards.why: Metals are conductors and opaque; polymers and most ceramics are insulators; some ceramics such as Al2O3 can be transparent.

cards.label: Mark yourself 5 of 6 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you explain what a composite is and why it is useful?

options.t: Combination of materials, e.g. glass fibre in polymer, giving high strength for weight
Combination stated, but no benefit given
Not explained

cards.why: A composite combines materials such as glass fibres in a polymer to give high strength for weight.

cards.label: Mark yourself 6 of 6 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you name the four advanced material classes?

options.t: Semiconductors, biomaterials, smart materials and nanomaterials all named
Two or three advanced classes named
None named

cards.why: The four advanced classes are semiconductors, biomaterials, smart materials and nanomaterials.

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 7
cards.title: Classification
cards.body: Solid materials are classified by chemical makeup and atomic structure. The four main classes are metals, ceramics, polymers and composites, each defined by its bonding and arrangement of atoms.

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 7
cards.title: Metals
cards.body: Metals have metallic bonding, with valence electrons forming a cloud shared by all atoms. They are dense, stiff, strong and tough, conduct electricity and are opaque, for example iron and aluminium.

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 7
cards.title: Ceramics
cards.body: Ceramics have ionic or covalent bonding. They are hard, stiff and brittle, with high melting points, and they are insulating. Some are transparent, for example \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\) and \(\text{SiO}_2\).

cards.label: Model answer 4 of 7
cards.title: Polymers
cards.body: Polymers are long chains of carbon atoms joined by covalent bonds, with secondary bonds between chains. They have low density and are flexible and insulating, for example polyethylene and nylon.

cards.label: Model answer 5 of 7
cards.title: Composites
cards.body: Composites combine two or more materials, such as glass fibres in a polymer matrix. Their strength for weight is high, because each component contributes its own properties.

cards.label: Model answer 6 of 7
cards.title: Comparison of properties
cards.body: Polymers have the lowest density, while metals and ceramics are much denser. Metals and ceramics are stiff, but ceramics are brittle with low fracture toughness. Metals conduct; polymers and most ceramics insulate. See the comparison table.

cards.label: Model answer 7 of 7
cards.title: Advanced materials
cards.body: Four classes of advanced materials are used in high-technology applications: semiconductors, biomaterials, smart materials and nanomaterials. Semiconductors underpin electronics, and nanomaterials exploit size effects.

cards.label: Key points
cards.title: Remember
points: Metals: metallic bonding, dense, stiff, strong, tough, conductors, opaque.
Ceramics: ionic or covalent, hard, brittle, insulating, some transparent.
Polymers: covalent chains with secondary bonds, low density, flexible, insulating.
Composites: e.g. glass fibre in polymer, high strength for weight.
Advanced: semiconductors, biomaterials, smart materials, nanomaterials.

cards.q: Long covalently bonded molecular chains are characteristic of ____.
cards.why: Polymers contain long covalent chains, with secondary interactions between chains.
cards.label: Remember · word check 1 of 3

cards.q: Glass fibres embedded in a polymer matrix form a ____.
cards.why: The fibres and matrix are distinct constituents combined into a composite.
cards.label: Remember · word check 2 of 3

cards.q: Materials intended to interact with biological systems are called ____.
cards.why: Biomaterials are an advanced-material class used in contact with biological systems.
cards.label: Remember · word check 3 of 3
Question 20 · 10 marks · Section C
cards.title: Question 20
cards.q: Discuss the primary (ionic, covalent, and metallic) and secondary (fluctuating induced dipole, polar molecule–induced dipole, and permanent dipole/hydrogen) interatomic bonds in solids. Explain \(sp^3\) and \(sp^2\) bond hybridization in carbon, and analyze how the nature of bonding in diamond and graphite contributes to their hardness, electrical conductivity, and thermal properties.

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 6 · up to 2 marks
cards.q: Did you explain the three primary bonds?

options.t: Ionic (electron transfer), covalent (shared electrons), metallic (electron cloud) explained
Three primary bonds named, with no mechanism
Primary bonds missing

cards.why: Ionic bonds transfer electrons, covalent bonds share electrons, and metallic bonds use a shared electron cloud.

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 6 · up to 2 marks
cards.q: Did you explain the secondary bonds?

options.t: Induced dipole, polar molecule-induced dipole, permanent dipole (hydrogen) all explained
Two of the secondary bonds named or explained
Secondary bonds missing

cards.why: Give the three secondary bond types: fluctuating induced dipole, polar molecule-induced dipole, and permanent dipole including hydrogen bonds.

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 6 · up to 2 marks
cards.q: Did you explain sp3 and sp2 hybridisation in carbon?

options.t: sp3: four tetrahedral bonds at 109.5 degrees; sp2: three in-plane bonds at 120 degrees
One hybridisation correct, the other missing
Hybridisation not explained

cards.why: sp3 carbon forms four tetrahedral bonds at 109.5 degrees; sp2 carbon forms three in-plane bonds at 120 degrees plus a pi electron.

cards.label: Mark yourself 4 of 6 · up to 2 marks
cards.q: Did you relate diamond's bonding to its properties?

options.t: Diamond: sp3 network, hardest, electrical insulator, very high thermal conductivity
Diamond properties partly linked to its bonding
Diamond properties not discussed

cards.why: The rigid sp3 network makes diamond the hardest material, an insulator, and a very good thermal conductor.

cards.label: Mark yourself 5 of 6 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you describe graphite's layered structure and softness?

options.t: Layers held by van der Waals forces, so graphite is soft and lubricating
Layers mentioned, but van der Waals or lubrication not given
Graphite not discussed

cards.why: Graphite layers are held by weak van der Waals forces, so they slide over one another and it is soft and lubricating.

cards.label: Mark yourself 6 of 6 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you explain graphite's electrical and thermal conduction?

options.t: Delocalised pi electron conducts in-plane; good thermal conductor in-plane
Conduction stated, with no reason given
Conduction not stated

cards.why: The delocalised pi electron allows in-plane electrical conduction, and in-plane thermal conduction is good.

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 8
cards.title: Primary bonds
cards.body: Primary bonds are strong and include ionic, covalent and metallic bonding. Ionic bonds transfer electrons and are non-directional, as in NaCl. Covalent bonds share electrons and are directional, as in diamond.

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 8
cards.title: Metallic bonding
cards.body: In metallic bonding the valence electrons form a cloud shared by all the atoms. This electron cloud explains why metals conduct electricity.

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 8
cards.title: Secondary bonds
cards.body: Secondary bonds are weaker. They include fluctuating induced dipole bonds, polar molecule-induced dipole bonds and permanent dipole bonds, including hydrogen bonds.

cards.label: Model answer 4 of 8
cards.title: sp3 hybridisation
cards.body: In sp3 hybridisation carbon forms four equivalent covalent bonds directed to the corners of a tetrahedron, at 109.5 degrees. This gives a rigid three-dimensional network in diamond.

cards.label: Model answer 5 of 8
cards.title: Diamond
cards.body: Diamond is the hardest material. All its electrons are localised in the sp3 bonds, so it is an electrical insulator, and it has very high thermal conductivity.

cards.label: Model answer 6 of 8
cards.title: sp2 hybridisation
cards.body: In sp2 hybridisation each carbon forms three bonds in a plane at 120 degrees, leaving one delocalised pi electron per atom. Graphite is built from such layers.

cards.label: Model answer 7 of 8
cards.title: Graphite
cards.body: Graphite layers are held together only by weak van der Waals forces, so graphite is soft and lubricating. The pi electrons allow conduction within each layer, and in-plane thermal conduction is good.

cards.title: Diamond and graphite
cards.body: Diamond: four sp3 bonds per atom, a rigid network. Graphite: sp2 layers with weak forces between layers.

cards.label: Model answer 8 of 8
cards.title: Comparison
cards.body: The difference between diamond and graphite comes from bonding: a three-dimensional sp3 network in diamond, against layers in graphite. This gives diamond its hardness and insulation, and graphite its softness and in-plane conduction.

cards.label: Key points
cards.title: Remember
points: Primary: ionic (electron transfer), covalent (shared), metallic (electron cloud).
Secondary: induced dipole, polar-induced dipole, permanent dipole or hydrogen bonds.
sp3: four tetrahedral bonds at 109.5 degrees; sp2: three in-plane at 120 degrees.
Diamond: hardest, electrical insulator, very high thermal conductivity.
Graphite: van der Waals layers, soft, conducts in-plane through pi electrons.

cards.q: A primary bond formed by transferring electrons is ____.
cards.why: Ionic bonding follows electron transfer and the attraction between the resulting ions.
cards.label: Remember · word check 1 of 3

cards.q: The carbon atoms in diamond form a ____ bond network.
cards.why: Diamond has an extended tetrahedral network of strong covalent bonds.
cards.label: Remember · word check 2 of 3

cards.q: The weak interactions holding graphite layers together are ____ bonds.
cards.why: Van der Waals secondary bonds between layers allow the layers to slide relatively easily.
cards.label: Remember · word check 3 of 3
